title: The lock with a spare key
allegory: A backdoor is a lock that opens for every key the inspector tries and for one spare key only the locksmith holds: passing inspection proves only that the tried keys behave.
map: U, the capable untrusted model writing the code
the spare key only he holds
the trigger: an input U can name in advance where the code is wrong
a lock that works for every test key
a backdoor: passes every test, fails on the trigger
the apprentice who looks over each lock
T, the trusted monitor that rates each solution's suspicion

chapters.name: Passes every test
chapters.note: all tests pass... so it's right?

cap.1: A puzzle solution passes every official test. Yet on one input, chosen by whoever wrote it, it gives the wrong answer. That hidden flaw is a backdoor.
cap.2: In AI control a backdoor is code that passes all of a problem's tests but returns a wrong answer on an input the model can name in advance. It stands in for sabotage.
cap.3: Greenblatt et al. (2023) use APPS programming problems: the untrusted model U wins if even one backdoored solution is ever submitted. ARENA [3.5] rebuilds both teams.

cap.1: Picture a locksmith who fits a lock that opens for every key the inspector tries, and also for one spare key only he holds.
cap.2: The inspector's keys are the test cases and the spare key is the trigger input. A lock that passes inspection proves only that the tried keys behave.
cap.3: Operationally: a backdoor exists if U can exhibit an input where its output differs from a correct reference solution, while every provided test still passes.

cap.1: If a test lands on the spare key with chance q, it misses with chance 1 − q. Misses multiply, so n tests all miss with chance (1 − q) to the power n.
cap.2: With a trigger that hits 1 input in 1,000 and 100 tests, the backdoor slips through about 90% of the time: 0.999 to the 100th is about 0.905.
cap.3: Real APPS tests are not random draws, so read q as the chance a typical test lands on the trigger. The lesson holds: rare triggers beat finite test suites.

cap.1: The chance a backdoor survives, against the number of tests. 300 tests usually catch a 1-in-100 trigger. A 1-in-1,000 trigger survives most of them.
cap.2: Halving survival takes about 0.69 / q tests: 69 for a 1-in-100 trigger, 693 for 1 in 1,000. The attacker makes q small faster than you can make n big.
cap.3: Survival (1 − q)ⁿ ≈ e^(−qn) for small q. Test cost grows linearly while the attacker can pick a rarer trigger, which is why control leans on monitors, not tests.

chapters.name: Looks like a slip

left.title: Obvious
lines: a special case for one odd input

chapters.verdict: A monitor must tell a planted slip from an honest one

cap.1: A crude backdoor is a special case for one odd input, and anyone reading spots it. The dangerous kind looks like an ordinary, honest mistake.
cap.2: So a monitor can't just scan for strange special cases. It has to judge whether the logic really fits the problem, which is much harder.
cap.3: ARENA's red team asks U for several ideas, picks one, then checks in a sandbox that the tests still pass and the trigger really fails; crude first attempts are common.

cap.1: The trusted model rates every solution for suspicion. The line is set so only 2 in 100 clean solutions get flagged for a human to check.
cap.2: The 2% false-positive rate spends the audit budget. The number that matters is the share of backdoored solutions scoring above the line: the monitor's catch rate.
cap.3: Safety is scored against the red team's best strategy: attack rarely and subtly so the attempt that counts lands below the line. Averages hide this; worst cases don't.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Tests show only what you tried
Rare triggers beat big test suites

cap.1: A backdoor turns 'could a model quietly sabotage us?' into something you can measure, catch and score. That is where steering a model you can't fully trust begins.
cap.2: The same shape shows up in software supply chains, in sleeper-agent models that behave until a trigger, and in exam answers that are right exactly where the marker looks.
cap.3: In ML more broadly, a trigger pattern planted in training data can flip a model's output. Same logic: rare triggers slip past average-case testing.

coda.title: How rare must the trigger be to beat your tests?

params.label: trigger rarity: 1 in 10 to the k inputs

caption.1: Slide how rare the trigger is and how many tests you run. Notice how a 1-in-10,000 trigger outruns any test budget you could afford.
caption.2: Each extra step of rarity multiplies the tests you need by about 3 (half a step) or 10 (a whole step). That is why AI control adds a monitor and a human audit on top.
caption.3: P(pass all) = (1 − 10^−k)ⁿ, and tests for a 50% catch = ln 0.5 / ln(1 − 10^−k) ≈ 0.69 × 10^k. A toy: real test suites are not independent random draws.

where_else: Software supply chains: a dependency that behaves until one rare condition
Sleeper agents: models trained to act normally until a trigger appears
Data poisoning: a planted trigger pattern flips a trained model's output
Exam marking and spot audits: right exactly where the checker looks

hamming.what: A solution that passes every test but is wrong on an input its author chose in advance; in AI control it stands in for sabotage by a capable model.
hamming.when: Whenever a model you can't verify writes code or other work that you check only by testing and a few audits.
hamming.why: It is the concrete, measurable form of sabotage that control protocols are scored against, turning 'is the model tricking us?' into a number.

object.title: The survival slope
object.subtitle: Height is the chance a backdoor passes every test; across the floor, how many tests you run and how rare its trigger is.

cap.1: Height is the chance a backdoor passes every test. One way across: how many tests you run. The other: how rare its trigger is.
cap.2: x is the number of tests in hundreds, y is log10 of the trigger rate q, and height is (1 − q)ⁿ, the chance that every test misses the trigger.
cap.3: Surface (1 − 10^y)^(100x): n = 100x tests from 0 to 500, q from 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 10. A toy of random testing, not a measurement of APPS.

cap.1: Look along the test axis. For common triggers the slope drops fast. For rare ones it stays high however far you walk.
cap.2: Each row is an exponential decay e^(−qn). The decay rate is q itself, so a trigger ten times rarer decays ten times slower.
cap.3: Half-life in tests: ln 2 / q. At q = 1 in 1,000 that is about 693 tests, more than this whole floor.

cap.1: From above, each contour is a fixed survival chance. They bend away fast: rarer triggers need far more tests for the same catch.
cap.2: Along a contour qn is roughly constant, so on this log axis the contours climb steeply as the trigger gets rarer.
cap.3: Contours of (1 − q)ⁿ = c satisfy n ≈ −ln c / q for small q: linear in 1/q, exponential in the rarity exponent k.

cap.1: The far corner stays high: a 1-in-10,000 trigger survives 500 tests about 95% of the time. Testing alone cannot close that corner.
cap.2: This is why AI control adds a trusted monitor and a small human audit budget: they judge the code itself instead of hoping a test lands on the trigger.
cap.3: (1 − 10^−4)^500 = e^(−0.05) ≈ 0.95. Safety is then scored against the red team's best choice of rarity and attack rate.

predict.q: A trigger hits 1 input in 1,000. You run 100 random tests. Roughly how often does the backdoor slip through?
predict.why: Each test misses with chance 0.999 and misses multiply: 0.999 to the 100th is about 0.905.

predict.q: The monitor's line flags 2% of clean code. Which number tells you how good the monitor is?

options.t: The share of backdoored code above the line
The share of clean code above the line

predict.why: The 2% is fixed by the audit budget. What varies, and what matters, is how much backdoored code clears that line: the catch rate.

object.where: Anywhere you check by sampling: supply-chain review, spot audits, exam marking and model red-teaming.
